items.title: Even Good Friends Can Be Bad Texters
items.description: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight. Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning. “Forgive the bad texters,” Julie Beck wrote in a recent Atlantic essay. Beck is one of them: She routinely leaves messages unanswered for days or even weeks, not because she doesn’t care but because she gets distracted, is burned-out, or simply forgets. Yet in a world where everyone is expected to be constantly reachable, a delayed reply can easily be mistaken for indifference. Texting has made staying in touch easier than ever, but it has also turned communication into a near-constant obligation. A third of Americans report feeling overwhelmed by the number of texts they need to respond to, Beck writes. People have felt guilty about unanswered correspondence for centuries, but technology has escalated both those expectations and the anxiety that comes with meeting them. Being a good texter, Beck suggests, isn’t the same as being a good friend. Someone who takes days to reply might still be the first to show up when you need them. So the next time a friend leaves you on read, consider giving them the benefit of the doubt. And if you’re the one with a growing pile of unanswered messages, maybe give yourself a little grace too. The Texting Trap Forgive the Bad Texters By Julie Beck We are truly sorry for our delayed response. Read the article. The Agony of Texting With Men By Matthew Schnipper Many guys are bad at messaging their friends back—and it might be making them more lonely. ( From 2025 ) Read the article. Another Symptom of Growing Isolation By Olga Khazan A recent study found that people spoke fewer words a day in 2019 than in 2005. Read the article. Still Curious? Would you go back to a time before smartphones if you could? In this episode of How to Touch Grass , Natalie Brennan and Julie Beck explore what’s behind analog nostalgia—and what it means for our relationship with technology in the future. The tension that defines modern life : Most people have a smartphone. But many want to use it less, Beck writes. Other Diversions “The nobel laureate who rescued me” The children of philanderers, by Tom Junod The marriage that captures a high point of American art PS Courtesy of Nancy C. My colleague Isabel Fattal recently asked readers to share a photo of something that sparks their sense of awe in the world. “About ten years ago, I saw a Joro spider for the first time. They are an invasive species from Asia. Since that time, they have become ubiquitous in my area,” Nancy C. from Marietta, Georgia, writes. “Last year I began to notice how incredibly beautiful the adult female spiders are. Their abdomens have a gorgeous, intricate design that looks like a colorful maze. I realized that for years, I had been walking by such sublime beauty, and I hadn’t even recognized it.” We’ll continue to feature your responses in the coming weeks. — Rafaela

items.title: Megyn Kelly’s Extreme Makeover
items.description: Do you remember Megyn Kelly? I once walked past her in a Chicago O’Hare bathroom in 2016, shortly after Donald Trump had won his first presidential election, and was momentarily stopped in my tracks by both her nuclear-grade charisma and her pixie cut. For a woman to have short hair on Fox News, where Kelly was a star anchor at the time, seemed as seditious to the network’s established order as reading Judith Butler or Karl Marx live on air. But this was a moment during which Kelly seemed to be leaning into the role of crusader for women—speaking out about being sexually harassed by the former Fox News CEO Roger Ailes and so inflaming Trump with her rigorous questioning during one debate that he later insinuated on CNN that she must have had her period . All of which makes it so disconcerting, 10 years later, to see Kelly now, on her daily SiriusXM and YouTube show, cursing and sneering with long barrel curls and the gusto of someone hosting not a discussion of polling data but a Two Minutes Hate. “I’m just gonna be honest, she’s not the most attractive gal,” Kelly said on Monday, discussing the anonymous woman who has filed a lawsuit detailing her alleged gang rape at Cornell University. (The men named in the lawsuit have denied any wrongdoing.) “She’s extremely”—here Kelly screwed up her face in disgust—“ beefy in, like, her arms and her legs. She has a whole video online talking about her cankles. And she possibly enjoyed being admired. This is how women make these mistakes. Admired, wanted—some women even foolishly say loved —by these guys at Cornell. This is probably a first for her. She’s probably thrilled to be so admired because she clearly didn’t grow up the incredibly beautiful one.” [ Sophie Gilbert: Is college getting less safe for women? ] We’ve seen some drastic heel turns in the media over the past few decades, but none quite as morally appalling as a former self-described advocate for female empowerment suggesting that a woman in this situation might have craved the attention because no one would have wanted to have sex with her otherwise. (Not to mention the contentions that the woman Kelly seems to be referring to, whose name has been leaked by some commentators, is not actually Jane Doe, based on her age and the fact that she would have been too young at the time to attend college.) Normally, I have a pretty strong constitution for this kind of bad-faith rage bait. But Kelly’s display this week of what I can describe only as performative hysteria has been hard to watch. Less than a minute into her show on Monday, she invoked the Salem witch trials. Twenty-three minutes in came her first pronounced use of the word fuck (I counted seven in total). That the whole performance was interspersed with ad reads for supplements and a tiny avatar of Kelly pointing giddily at the “Subscribe” button just added to the cognitive dissonance. It felt like watching morning television in Gilead. I’ve been stuck all week on the question of how much of Kelly’s performance these days is attention-seeking behavior for the YouTube algorithm and how much is reflective of what she actually believes. Kelly, 55, grew up outside of Albany, where she also went to law school, becoming an editor at the Albany Law Review . She was an attorney for almost a decade, but has said that watching live newscasts on 9/11 inspired her to change careers and become a TV reporter. She was hired full-time at Fox News in 2004. Before long—according to her allegations—Ailes began making inappropriate comments, such as how sexy he imagined her bras must be. In January 2006, Kelly claimed, Ailes tried to kiss her; after his third attempt, she said she got up and walked out of his office. (Ailes denied Kelly’s allegations; he died in 2017.) Three months later, Kelly made a name for herself with her skeptical coverage of the Duke lacrosse team’s alleged gang rape of an erotic dancer. (The woman in question eventually admitted to fabricating the assault.) All of this matters, I think, because it communicates to what extent Kelly’s apparent worldview—where she herself can face sexual harassment due to patriarchal power structures that protect and even reward abusive men, but other women are likely lying—has been shaped by her rise and fall on TV news. In 2016, she declined in an interview with NPR to call herself a feminist. (She dislikes the label, she said, as though it’s just a branding issue.) Her 2016 book, Settle for More , was published just a week after Trump won the presidential election, and became a No. 1 New York Times best seller. Reviews were lukewarm, perhaps because of the news environment: “For all the disgust that she claims to feel for the misogyny and male entitlement” that seemed to be ramping back up in the national culture, Isaac Chotiner wrote in Slate , “and for all the personal harm it caused her, our bleak future is one in which Megyn Kelly is likely to find herself right at home.” But things took a downward turn when Kelly left the Fox fold. In 2017 she was poached by NBC News, which offered her an annual salary reported to be more than $20 million to host a daytime talk show, Megyn Kelly Today , and a Sunday-night news magazine, which was criticized for softball interviews with Vladimir Putin and Alex Jones and ultimately canceled. Megyn Kelly Today didn’t fare much better—Kelly, with her flinty self-possession, was criticized for being too chilly for daytime TV. During her first week, she awkwardly grilled Jane Fonda about whether she’d had plastic surgery while Fonda was promoting a movie next to her co-star Robert Redford. (“We really want to talk about that?” Fonda responded, after an agonizing few seconds of icy silence.) In October 2018, Megyn Kelly Today was canceled when Kelly defended blackface in a segment on Halloween costumes. Soon, she was dropped by her agency, CAA. A few months later, her NBC contract expired. This moment seems to have influenced Kelly’s current persona. Public humiliation is hard for anyone to endure, but for someone with a renegade streak (“I’ve never been a ‘pc’ kind of person,” she reportedly wrote in her apology email to NBC staffers after her blackface comments), seeing so many people celebrating her failure must have been immensely painful. By the time The Megyn Kelly Show launched as a podcast in September 2020, mid-pandemic, Kelly was snidely describing her guests as lefties, complaining about the assault allegations against the Supreme Court justice Brett Kavanaugh, and raging at the “dishonesty” of the press covering Trump. The pivot, whatever its reason, seems to have done what it was supposed to. Kelly has more than 4 million YouTube subscribers and The Megyn Kelly Show is one of the top podcasts in the country. Because Kelly is half-Italian and half-Irish, she told Semafor in 2024, “if you choose to watch the show, you will definitely glean something from the hand gestures and facial expressions that you might not pick up from listening alone.” Having watched Kelly all week, I can attest to this. Although she injects real poison in her voice to rage against, say, the singer Olivia Rodrigo for expressing support for Cornell’s Jane Doe, she accompanies this with the shrugs and waves of a waiter trying to describe tonight’s special of veal parmigiana. “Olivia, in sum, you don’t know what the fuck you’re talking about,” she said. “Shut up and stick to singing. I liked you better when you were in front of a microphone singing your weird little depressing songs. Shut UP. You don’t know what you’re talking about.” You can sense she’s imagining clips being spliced for TikTok and Instagram, and tailoring her delivery to provoke maximum indignation. As a rant, it feels much too phony—and cynical, given how fury seems to be the sole emotion that can build an audience in 2026, and the fact that Rodrigo is one of the most popular women alive. (“The only reliable way to reach mainstream or even moderate recognition against all the noise,” Rebecca Jennings wrote earlier this year in New York magazine, “is to either carpet-bomb social media with clips or to enrage wide swaths of the public.”) But in moments, Kelly does seem to slip out of character. Although she seems perfectly happy excoriating Jane Doe, Kelly draws the line at revealing her name. “I know her name,” she said on Monday. “It’s been well publicized online. But no one in the mainstream media has said it. And as you know I’m seriously considering just saying it. And the reason I haven’t is because I don’t want to do anything to hurt this young woman, to get her hurt, or to add to the pain I’m sure she’s feeling.” Her voice is surprisingly gentle. Her hands stay down in her lap. Could it be that this woman who herself had to hire armed guards for her family after being personally targeted by Trump actually feels for someone caught in a similar nightmare? Is all this spewed-out ire and provocation really just about a reward as soul-rotting as clicks and followers? I don’t think Megyn Kelly will ever tell us, but I have my suspicions.

items.title: The Best Protein Source Is Hiding in Plain Sight
items.description: Somehow, America has yet to reach peak protein. Perhaps we never will. Even after David bars have gone viral for being bricks of essentially pure protein and Starbucks has rolled out lattes topped with “protein cold foam,” new and somehow weirder protein-laced products keep hitting shelves. You can now buy protein Honey Nut Cheerios, protein popcorn and PopCorners, protein sodas, protein ranch dressing, and protein chips. (Doritos launched a nacho-cheese-flavored version with 10 grams of protein per one-ounce serving.) In an era of GLP-1 drugs and peptide stacks and Oura rings and self-optimization, of wellness influencers and looks-maxxers, everybody seems to be doing everything they can to eat as much protein as possible. The magical macronutrient will supposedly make you more muscular, or more toned, or thinner—or something, really anything, just better . Amid the protein frenzy, regular food seemingly doesn’t cut it anymore. Why order a simple flat white when you can instead sip a Dunkin’ Nutty Pumpkin Iced Protein Latte? [ Read: America has entered late-stage protein ] Into the fray, I would suggest a humble alternative: Have some yogurt. Calorie for calorie, Greek yogurt has more protein than Chipotle’s High Protein Low Calorie Bowl, Kraft’s new PowerMac, or yes, a Dunkin’ Nutty Pumpkin Iced Protein Latte. So do some traditional yogurts, as well as other fermented options in the dairy aisle such as skyr and kefir. And that’s if you opt for the full-fat, luscious kind (which I recommend). Nonfat Greek yogurt, which is lower in calories, is roughly as protein-dense as a David bar—with the added benefits of having just two ingredients (milk, culture) and not tasting like plastic. Yogurt is not only full of protein but also good for your bones, your digestion, and your immune system. Yogurt is an ingredient: Eat it plain or bake with it, use it as the base of a sauce or dip, throw it in a marinade or soup. Sure, some yogurts have added sugars , but so does a Starbucks Iced Banana Protein Cream Matcha. And as far as health fads go, yogurt is typically probiotic . All things considered, yogurt may be the easiest protein of all. [ Read: Let’s not fool ourselves about yogurt ] In spite of everything it has going for it, yogurt has not been the face of the protein craze. Perhaps that’s because yogurt is not splashy or technologically innovative or referred to by a trademarked proper noun. A David bar may taste different and have distinct packaging from an RxBar or a Jacob protein bar made with beef tallow, but all plain yogurt is the same. Though some companies have released “protein-enhanced” yogurt (whatever that means), for the most part yogurt is not optimized by corporate food scientists and focus groups in the way that today’s protein-branded products are. Yogurt has been optimized in the sense that humans have consumed it for thousands of years. Imagine wellness influencers suggesting that you dollop yogurt into a bowl and sprinkle berries on top without measuring anything. There wouldn’t be any regimen to adopt or wellness plan to pay for. There wouldn’t be any special trademarked protein products for influencers to hawk: The company behind the David bar, for instance, has sponsored Andrew Huberman and, until recently, Peter Attia was its chief science officer. The homemade parfait would all be rather mundane and boring compared with Attia’s rotation of four protein powders or the bodybuilder Chris Bumstead’s breakfast filet mignon. It wouldn’t get any views. Protein is not just a health fad; it is a business. So is everything else in the world of wellness. Indeed, there’s something about many of these setups—which proffer the perfect low-calorie, high-protein snack to pick up on your way to work every morning; a biometric wristband to wear every night; supplements to consume every day for the rest of your life; a weight-loss drug you will inject every week—that keeps people coming back for more, giving their attention and money and energy to the endless pursuit of betterment. Health and more broadly self-improvement are, obviously, admirable pursuits. Protein can be a way to achieve either. But obsessing over hitting those goals can become unhealthy, as most obsessions are. Have some yogurt, or don’t. You’ll probably be fine.

items.title: ‘Elon Is a Nuke’
items.description: In December 2021, Elon Musk sat for an interview with The Babylon Bee , a conservative satire site. Having covered the typical topics (wokeness, free speech, Elizabeth Warren) and finding themselves with a bit more time to fill, the outlet’s then–creative director closed out the chat with a request. “ The Babylon Bee is a Christian organization, and we’re a ministry,” he reminded Musk. So “we’re wondering if you could do us a quick solid and accept Jesus as your lord and savior?” Musk laughed. The others did too. The guys waited for an answer, and Musk, after rambling a bit, gave one. Sure, he replied with a shrug—why not? “If Jesus is saving people,” he said, “I mean, I won’t stand in his way.” The exchange makes a brief but incredibly effective appearance in Musk , the documentarian Alex Gibney’s new film: Asked for a come-to-Jesus moment, Musk professes his faith in himself. The Musk of 2021 was considerably less consequential than the Musk of today. He had not yet added Twitter—humanity’s “collective consciousness,” he once called it—to his portfolio, nor had he staged his hostile takeover of the United States government or become the world’s first trillionaire . Still, Musk had slightly more reason than most to assume his high status on the cosmic org chart. Through Tesla and Starlink and SpaceX, his dominion stretched over the heavens and the Earth. Through Neuralink and his assorted experiments with artificial intelligence, Musk was expanding his reach into human hearts and minds. As a media figure, too, he was all but inescapable: a piece of software downloaded into people’s lives whether they had opted in to him or not. Power, at that sort of scale, changes every equation. It can make hyperbole seem accurate. It can make a man, small and flawed, look like something more: a genius, an idol, an outlet for everyday faith. And the discrepancy between the person Musk is and the figure he claims to be is one of Musk ’s running themes. The man sells himself as a savior; many have before. But he is where he is—he is what he is—because so many people have bought into the pitch. Delusions of grandeur are one thing. The real trouble comes when one person’s delusions become other people’s reality. [ Read: Maybe Alex Gibney did Elon Musk a favor ] Musk benefits, appropriately enough, from an exercise in data science. The man himself did not participate; he declined Gibney’s overtures in the most Muskian manner imaginable: through an insult-laden post on X. As a work-around, the director and his team created a database compiling every comment Musk has been recorded making in public. That data set—a galaxy-brained version of Musk—informed their assessment of him and individual moments in the film. Muskisms (about the likelihood that earthly life is a simulation, about the drawbacks of empathy, about humans’ future on Mars) make their way into the proceedings via a computer-generated version of Musk—an animated character who appears where, in a traditional documentary, Gibney might have quoted his subject. To an extent, the approach turns the tables on Musk. It renders this person who talks fondly of humans’ cyborgian future as a cartoonishly uncanny, flagrantly inhuman presence. But it also highlights his cultural status as a man who is, at this point, something more than just a man. The sources that Musk cites as it creates its portrait—among them the people who have worked with and lived with and, often, clashed with Musk—regularly mention the scale of his ego and the scope of his ambition. They attribute much of his success to his mythmaking capabilities: his romantic descriptions of technology, his branding of consumer goods as spiritual necessities. Tesla, Musk’s car company, “is not automobile manufacturing or automobile retailing,” the financial analyst Lawrence Fossi tells Gibney. “This is not finance”; instead, he says, it is religion. The mythology extends to Musk himself. “In Elon We Trust,” one of Musk’s followers once tweeted at him, in a post Gibney included in the film. Another informed him, “We follow you like a cult :).” [ Read: We are living in the fantasy world of 13-year-old boys ] A former girlfriend says in the film that Musk likes to compare himself to Kublai Khan, the 13th-century Mongolian warrior and emperor of China. And indeed, his megalomania is in one way a very old story: Human history has, for better and worse, been shaped by men who insisted on their godlike supremacy. But Musk’s version is also thoroughly modern. His power is systemic. His sieges rise from within. One of the allegations the film makes against Musk concerns his incursion into the U.S. government: DOGE’s haphazard dismantling of government agencies, its destruction of scientific research, its toppling of USAID. The widespread effects of DOGE’s efforts—the cures that won’t be found; the vaccines that won’t be made; the food meant to save lives , left instead to rot—will likely never be fully known. Nevertheless, Musk argues, the raid has had a death toll: hundreds of thousands of people, and potentially many more. When such accusations are made, the public might ask, and should ask, what accountability looks like at that level. But one of the affordances of planet-spanning power is that it can turn justice, as most people experience it, into something of a joke. If Musk is a category error incarnate—a man with, effectively, a gross national product; a guy whose influence extends beyond the stratosphere—the confusion does more than elevate him. It also helps inoculate him. The film quotes a newscaster’s summary of one of SpaceX’s early launches. “Only four entities have launched a space capsule into orbit and successfully brought it back to the Earth,” the reporter announces: “the United States, Russia, China, and Elon Musk.” How do you make sense of that kind of power? How do you challenge it? One truism of modern life is that humans, as animals who would prefer to pretend that they are otherwise, were not made to thrive at our current scale. We weren’t meant to know this many people, to process this much information, to make sense of a world that stretches so far beyond our immediate grasp. Musk provides a corollary to those claims: It gives us a human who himself has become too colossal to make sense of, too unwieldy to respond to. Even more than his fellow tech titans , Musk exists at a scale that no man was able to before and enjoys power so complete that it becomes self-ratifying. No man should be so godlike. No person should be so exceptional. In the film, Musk’s former girlfriend sums up the matter concisely: “Elon is a nuke,” she says—a human of mass destruction.

items.title: Glut! Farmers count losses as prices crash, customers happy
items.description: Farmers of vegetables in the Nabdam District of the Upper East Region are counting their losses as a sharp decline in the prices of tomatoes, pepper and okra threatens to undermine their incomes. The prices of the vegetables have dropped significantly within the past month, following what farmers described as an increase in supply as more farmers bring their produce to the market. Market survey A market survey conducted by the Daily Graphic at the three major markets in Nabdam, including Pelungu, Kongo and Zanlerigu, showed that the price of a bucket of tomatoes had fallen from between GH¢120 and GH¢150 at the beginning of September this year to between GH¢60 and GH¢70 in early October. Similarly, a basin of tomatoes, which previously sold for between GH¢300 and GH¢350, was now selling for between GH¢120 and GH¢150. The prices of okra and fresh pepper had also declined sharply. A bucket of okra, which previously sold for about GH¢120, was now going for GH¢80, while a bucket of fresh pepper was being sold between GH¢100 and GH¢120, as against the GH¢150 and GH¢200 recorded in September. Farmers count losses The development has brought some relief to consumers but has left farmers worried about recovering the huge investments they made in producing the vegetables. Farmers attributed the situation to an increase in the supply of vegetables, saying the abundance of produce had weakened their bargaining power in the markets. A tomato farmer, Mboleni Zoya, expressed frustration over the situation, saying the prevailing prices did not reflect the cost of producing the vegetables. “We are not happy with the current prices, considering our expenses. However, with tomatoes being perishable, we are forced to sell at whatever price we can when there is abundance. This is the time most of us are harvesting because we all depend on the rain, and that is why you are seeing tomatoes all over with few buyers,” he said. Another tomato and pepper farmer, Samson Wougnab, said the falling prices were discouraging, emphasising that farmers would struggle to break even if the trend continued. “We were happy when a bucket was around GH¢150 or above because that would have helped us cover our expenditure, but now we are not even breaking even with the current prices.” Buyers will intentionally come and wait until around 11 a.m. or 12 noon, and they come in with their own prices. If you don’t agree, you have to send it back home because they can’t even finish buying it,” he said. High production costs The farmers said the sharp decline in prices was particularly worrying because the cost of production remained high. They cited increasing expenditure on labour, seedlings, fertiliser and other farm inputs as some of the major costs affecting their profitability. Mr Wougnab stated that, “During the beginning of the season, a bag of fertiliser was between GH¢450 and GH¢500, and a labourer was paid between GH¢70 and GH¢80. Even putting my daily routine on the farm aside, imagine selling a bucket of tomatoes for GH¢60 or GH¢70, which is even in rare cases because sometimes you just have to give it out for something small. So, we are losing a lot.” Mixed fortunes While farmers complained about the situation, some food vendors and consumers welcomed the reduction in prices. A food vendor, Ateni Ababila, said fluctuations in vegetable prices made it difficult for traders to predict their profit margins. “For instance, buying a bucket of tomatoes for GH¢50 in Pelungu and transporting it to Bolgatanga at an additional GH¢10, only to sell it for less than GH¢80, means we end up with little or no profit. Sometimes, we are forced to sell it at a lower price because we cannot store it,” she said. However, another food vendor at the Pelungu Market, Yenmah Mba, said the lower prices had improved her profit margins. “The lower prices have led to substantial profits for me, and I hope this trend continues because this is normally the season for us to also enjoy. By the end of December, prices will rise, and by January, we won’t get enough to buy in the district. So, let us enjoy it. Even if we get a bucket for GH¢40, we want it,” she said. A customer, who is a teacher, also expressed satisfaction with the price reductions, saying they had made it possible for consumers to buy more vegetables with relatively little money. “The reduced prices are fantastic. Now, a small amount of money can buy what I need, which is a significant improvement. It is time for us to also enjoy our stew at a lesser cost, but we are sorry for the farmers, though,” she said. Call for support The seasonal harvesting of vegetables and other crops in the Upper East Region usually increases from September and continues into the latter part of the year, resulting in increased supplies of some farm produce on local markets. The Upper East Regional Director of Agriculture, Alhaji Fuseini Zakaria, said most of the farmers relied on rain for production. “Over 90 per cent of the farmers rely on rain, so what it means is that they start planting at the same time, and that is the result we are seeing now. If there is support for them to have mechanised boreholes, that will be appreciated because it tells you that when these farmers are given the needed support to produce year-round, we won’t have problems with vegetables at any time in the season,” he said.

items.title: Agadez : quatre groupes électrogènes prévus pour renforcer l’approvisionnement électrique…
items.description: Le Niger prévoit d’acheminer à court terme quatre groupes électrogènes de 3 MW chacun, soit une capacité supplémentaire de 12 MW, pour améliorer la desserte électrique dans la région d’Agadez, a annoncé mercredi 7 octobre 2026 le ministère de l’Énergie. Le ministre de l’Énergie, le Colonel Seyni Alzouma, a entamé le même jour une mission dans la région. Il s’est rendu à la centrale NIGELEC de Toudou et à la centrale hybride d’Agadez afin d’évaluer les installations et les besoins de la zone nord. Les études de faisabilité pour l’installation des nouveaux groupes sont en cours. Une centrale solaire de 7 MW avec stockage est également en construction. Selon le ministère, 12 915 panneaux ont déjà été installés et les travaux sont réalisés à 55 %. La pose devrait être achevée dans environ deux mois. Les besoins en électricité d’Agadez, d’Arlit et de Tchirozérine sont estimés à 26 MW, contre 3,8 MW de capacités thermiques disponibles à Agadez et Arlit, indique le ministère. Plus de 11 000 branchements ont par ailleurs été réalisés depuis janvier dans ces deux villes. Cette mission intervient alors que les coupures d’électricité perturbent les activités dans la région. Les autorités examinent aussi des mesures concernant les capacités de production et le réseau de distribution, ainsi que des projets de coopération entre le Niger et l’Algérie, dont la construction d’une centrale mobile et d’une centrale solaire. Source: Aïr-Info Agadez L’article Agadez : quatre groupes électrogènes prévus pour renforcer l’approvisionnement électrique… est apparu en premier sur Tamtaminfo .

items.title: Man charged with attempted murder after stabbing
items.description: A man has been charged with attempted murder following a stabbing incident in Borough Green in which three people were injured. Kent Police said armed officers were called to a property in Sevenoaks Road, at about 07:40 BST on Thursday. Two men suffered injuries consistent with stab wounds, and a woman sustained injuries to her arm and face. One of the men’s injuries was potentially life-changing, Kent Police said. Juan Martez-Ortiz has been charged with attempted murder, two counts of causing grievous bodily harm with intent, possession of a knife, aggravated burglary and stalking, the force said. Kent Police say the 46-year-old Dominican national, of Sevenoaks Road, has been remanded in custody and is due to appear at Maidstone Crown Court on Saturday.

World Cup visa scandal: Senyo Hosi says issue goes beyond calls for Sports Minister’s resignation
items.description: Convener of the OneGhana Movement and Trustee of the Ghana Coalition Against Galamsey, Senyo Hosi, has called for the controversy surrounding Ghana’s visa arrangements for the 2026 FIFA World Cup to be addressed as a matter of constitutional compliance and accountability, rather than focusing solely on whether the Sports Minister should resign. Mr Hosi said he was disappointed that Ghana appeared to be repeating past mistakes, warning that the issue had implications for the country’s reputation, public confidence and the values being passed on to future generations. He stressed that the controversy was not simply about visa processing but about whether public officials and administrative bodies were complying with the principles of probity, accountability and the rule of law. Citing Article 232 of the 1992 Constitution, which establishes the Commission on Human Rights and Administrative Justice (CHRAJ), he emphasised the importance of fairness, reasonableness and adherence to legal obligations in public administration. Mr Hosi also questioned what young people would learn if political parties condemned similar controversies while in opposition, only for comparable concerns to emerge when they assumed office. He said the Minority in Parliament was entitled to scrutinise the matter as part of its oversight responsibilities, although he urged its members to remain balanced and fair in their approach. His comments follow allegations by the Ranking Member on Parliament’s Youth and Sports Committee, Vincent Ekow Assafuah, that some individuals paid between US$7,000 and US$14,000 for visa processing linked to World Cup-related activities. The Minority has also questioned the verification of personnel lists submitted by the Ghana Tourism Authority (GTA) and the National Sports Authority (NSA) to the US and Canadian embassies. It alleged that only two of 50 names submitted by the GTA as media personnel were verified as professional media practitioners, while 15 of 102 names submitted by the NSA were confirmed as actual employees. President John Dramani Mahama has asked former NSA Director-General Yaw Ampofo Ankrah to step aside, with Professor Emmanuel Osei Sarpong appointed acting Director-General. The Ministry of Sports and Recreation has also provided a chronology of its engagements, citing correspondence dated January 28, 2026, which it says shows that some arrangements connected to the World Cup fan experience predated its involvement. Mr Hosi said Ghanaians should be able to trust their governments regardless of whether the New Patriotic Party or the National Democratic Congress is in power, urging public officials to uphold their responsibilities and work towards fulfilling citizens’ aspirations. He maintained that the priority should be to establish the facts, uphold constitutional standards and ensure accountability, rather than allow the controversy to become solely a political dispute over resignations.

items.title: L’Allemagne dépêche sa diplomate à Niamey pour negocier un partenariat « d’égal à égal »…

Reçue par le Premier ministre nigérien Ali Mahaman Lamine Zeine, la diplomate allemande est venue négocier la poursuite d’un dialogue bilatéral désormais dicté par les termes d’un partenariat souverain et d’égal à égal. Qualifiant l’entretien de « franc et amical », la représentante allemande a officiellement réaffirmé l’engagement de Berlin à maintenir ses liens historiques avec le Niger. Face à un Sahel affirmant de plus en plus sa puissance et imposant ses conditions sur place, la coopération bilatérale se concentrera exclusivement sur le développement civil et humanitaire, incluant l’agriculture, les infrastructures, la décentralisation et la cohésion sociale. items.title: Edouard Philippe et la relation France-Algérie : y a-t-il autre chose que l’accord de 1968 ?
items.description: Edouard Philippe , le candidat du centre-droite à l’élection présidentielle française de 2027, ne lâche pas l'accord franco-algérien de 1968 sur l’immigration. Il ne rate décidément pas une sortie pour réitérer sa promesse de révoquer ce traité qui régit depuis près de 60 ans l’entrée et le séjour des Algériens en France. L’ancien premier ministre d’Emmanuel Macron fait peut-être plus fort que Bruno Retailleau en la matière. Il en a encore longuement parlé jeudi soir sur France 2. C’est quasiment le sujet dont il parle quand il évoque les relations entre l’Algérie et la France. N’y a-t-il pas autre chose entre les deux pays que cet accord ? Edouard Philippe, un des premiers à appeler à dénoncer l’accord de 1968 Sur les questions liées à l’immigration, il est difficile de distinguer le programme de l'ancien Premier ministre de ceux des candidats de la droite dure et de l'extrême-droite. Sur l’Algérie, Philippe a même comme une obsession, et particulièrement pour l'accord de 1968. Il était l'un des tout premiers à soutenir l'idée de révoquer le traiter, lancée en 2023 par Xavier Driencourt, ancien ambassadeur de France en Algérie à deux reprises. “J'étais un des premiers à dire que, lorsque les traités anciens qui règlent la question de l’entrée et du séjour des étrangers en France n’étaient plus satisfaisants, il fallait les dénoncer”, a-t-il rappelé sur France 2, jeudi. “Je rétablis une relation de droit commun” “Je le dénonce et je rétablis une relation, en matière de droit à l’entrée et au séjour des étrangers algériens en France, de droit commun.”, a-t-il dit. Mettant l’Algérie dans le registre des pays “qui ne respectent pas le droit international et qui mettent en cause notre capacité à maîtriser l'immigration”, le maire du Havre a dit ne pas considérer qu'il y a dans la relation bilatérale aujourd'hui “quoi que ce soit qui justifie des stipulations particulières plus favorables pour les Algériens”, rappelle-t-il, “La politique de Macron vis-à-vis de l’Algérie n'est pas la mienne” Le candidat à la présidentielle de 2027 se démarque d’Emmanuel Macron, dont il fut Premier ministre : “Sa politique vis-à-vis de l’Algérie n'est pas la mienne. Beaucoup de présidents français, et pas seulement Emmanuel Macron, dans le passé ont considéré que pour normaliser la relation avec l'Algérie, il fallait faire des gestes, donner des gages, donner des assurances, créer des dispositions parfois plus favorables.” Même Nicolas Sarkozy “s’était engagé sur le même chemin” et, tous, “ils n’ont rien obtenu ce faisant”. “Ce n'est pas la voie à suivre dans notre relation diplomatique avec l’Algérie”, assène-t-il. “Je pense qu'il faut qu'on change notre manière de traiter avec l’Algérie qui est un grand pays, qui est un pays souverain, qu'on respecte, mais dont on ne peut pas accepter qu'il soit lié à la France par des dispositions plus favorables”, a soutenu le président du parti Horizons, toujours en parlant de l’accord de 1968 alors que les spécialistes du dossier dont les avocats Abderrazak Boudjelti et Fayçal Megherbi ont prouvé que cet accord a été vidé de sa substance. Ce qui n’empêche pas certains candidats de continuer à instrumentaliser à outrance, particulièrement Édouard Philippe qui en parle désormais plus que Bruno Retailleau ou Marine Le Pen. Dans son intervention, le candidat s’est engagé à réduire de moitié les flux de l’immigration légale pour revenir à moins de 200 000 entrées par an. L’article Edouard Philippe et la relation France-Algérie : y a-t-il autre chose que l’accord de 1968 ? est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Sport, santé et jeunesse : la Guinée lance la première édition du FESTIBEG, avec le Maroc comme pays invité d’honneur
items.description: À l’occasion d’un point de presse organisé ce vendredi 9 octobre dans les locaux du ministère des Sports, le Fonds d’aide au développement du sport (FADES) a officiellement présenté la première édition du Festival des sports et du bien-être de Guinée (FESTIBEG). L’événement se tiendra du 4 au 6 décembre prochain au stade Petit Sory de Nongo, avec le Royaume du Maroc à l’honneur en qualité de pays invité. Placée sous le thème « Simandou 2040: le bien-être par le sport », cette édition inaugurale proposera notamment une marche de santé de 5 km, une séance de fitness géant, des conseils en nutrition et en prévention, ainsi que des bilans médicaux gratuits, incluant le dépistage du diabète et le contrôle de la tension artérielle. Durant ces trois jours, le public aura l’opportunité de découvrir une grande diversité de disciplines sportives et d’activités culturelles, allant du football au basketball 3×3, en passant par le handball, un mini-tournoi de karaté, le tir à l’arc, l’escrime, le tennis de table, le scrabble ou encore le breakdance. Fatima Fakhry présente les activités prévues Prenant la parole pour détailler la substance de ce rassemblement, Fatima Fakhry, directrice générale de Fox Communication et responsable de la communication du FESTIBEG, a déclaré : « Le FADES a pensé associer le volet bien-être à travers une marche de 5 kilomètres, une séance de fitness géante, des conseils en nutrition et en prévention, ainsi que des bilans de santé gratuits portant notamment sur la tension, le poids et le diabète. Le festival s’articulera autour d'un village regroupant des stands d'exposition, des associations, des acteurs sportifs et des exposants de produits ou services liés au bien-être. » Poursuivant les échanges, Monson Sissoko a précisé le cadre et les objectifs fondamentaux de cette initiative : « Le Fonds d'Aide au Développement du Sport a pour mission de soutenir l'ensemble des projets et programmes de développement sportif en Guinée. Nos prérogatives incluent la promotion du sport à la base et du sport pour tous. Sachant qu'aujourd'hui 79 % de la population guinéenne est constituée de jeunes et face au constat que de nombreuses pathologies sont liées à la sédentarité et au manque de pratique sportive, nous avons conçu cet événement. Promouvoir le sport à la base, valoriser les métiers du sport et soutenir l'amélioration des infrastructures au niveau local sont des priorités auxquelles le Festibeg apporte une réponse concrete. » Le directeur du FADES espère que ce festival permettra de mettre en lumière le potentiel encore inexploité du secteur en Guinée. «Il s'agit d'échanger sur l'économie du sport, les infrastructures, les carrières sportives, la lutte contre le dopage et la promotion de la santé. Cette plateforme doit nous permettre de dégager des solutions innovantes pour le secteur. C'est cette ambition qui a motivé le FADES et ses partenaires à porter ce projet dont la Guinée a besoin […] Le Festibeg 2026 est un projet d'envergure nationale. Il traduit la volonté d'un pays d'investir dans son capital humain par le biais du sport et d'envoyer un signal fort à ses citoyens et à la communauté internationale ». S’exprimant sur instruction du ministre des Sports, Billy Keïta, secrétaire général du ministère des Sports, a, quant à lui, souligné l’impact socio-économique croissant du sport, vecteur de création d’emplois, d’entrepreneuriat et d’amélioration des conditions de vie, avant de réaffirmer le soutien institutionnel de l’État : « C'est de vous rassurer d'avance que le ministère sera présent avec ses directions et ses services tous derrière M. le ministre de sport pour faire de cet événement un événement d'une grandeur mature, qui sera très rassembleur et de montrer jusqu'au un tel festival permettrait un vrai développement. C'est vrai que FADES a impulsé l'initiative d'inviter les différentes structures, mais ensemble, c'est une fédération des forces pour aboutir à un résultat. Et c'est pourquoi le monsieur le ministre me charge de vous dire, chers journalistes, qu'il compte sur vous pour être présents et d'amplifier cet événement Il compte sur chaque guinéen et chaque guinéenne d'être au rendez-vous puisque plus que jamais aux côtés de ces différents services, il fera de cet événement l'un des plus grands jamais réalisé en matière du sport. » Mamadou Yaya Barry L’article Sport, santé et jeunesse : la Guinée lance la première édition du FESTIBEG, avec le Maroc comme pays invité d’honneur est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Yaw Ampofo Ankrah hasn’t taken or received any money to facilitate visas – Lawyer insists
items.description: The lawyer for the suspended Director-General of the National Sports Authority (NSA), Yaw Ampofo Ankrah, has insisted that his client has not received any money from individuals in connection with the alleged FIFA World Cup 2026 visa scandal. Yaw Ampofo Ankrah has been suspended from his position amid controversy over an alleged visa facilitation arrangement linked to the tournament. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, October 10, his lawyer, Jerry Avernugbor, said the Criminal Investigations Department (CID) was aggressively investigating the matter and urged the public to allow the process to establish the facts. “The police are investigating aggressively, and they’ve been investigating for the past whole week,” he said, adding that he and his client had been attending interviews at the CID headquarters. Mr Avernugbor maintained that his client had neither received money from applicants nor participated in any visa-related transactions. “What I’m saying here is, let it be known, my client has not received a penny from any individual,” he stressed. He explained that, during the investigation, he had seen documents relating to the allegations but cautioned against interpreting them without considering the full circumstances. According to him, the evidence available to investigators could lead to conclusions different from those being drawn from documents circulating publicly. The lawyer also said his client had been introduced to a company through a representative at the US Embassy, which he claimed had presented the company as a legitimate entity. He added that his client had designated an assistant as the point of contact after the embassy requested one. Mr Avernugbor acknowledged that the investigation could establish wrongdoing but insisted that any conclusions about his client’s involvement should be based on the evidence. “If my client is found guilty, the law will take its course, and the police are doing very, very well in this regard,” he said. He further indicated that the investigation would need to clarify the circumstances surrounding individuals alleged to have paid money in connection with the visa applications. The CID is investigating allegations of irregularities involving visa applications linked to Ghana’s participation in the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

Mr Hosi said Ghanaians should be able to trust their governments regardless of whether the New Patriotic Party or the National Democratic Congress is in power, insisting that public officials must work to fulfil citizens’ aspirations.

items.title: Pakistan and Azerbaijan reaffirm strategic partnership, vow closer economic ties
items.description: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday reaffirmed Pakistan’s “deep-rooted, fraternal and strategic partnership” with Azerbaijan during a telephone conversation with President Ilham Aliyev, the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said. According to the PMO, the two leaders reviewed bilateral ties and agreed to translate their strong political understanding into closer economic, investment and commercial cooperation. “The prime minister reaffirmed Pakistan’s deep-rooted, fraternal, and strategic partnership with Azerbaijan, characterised by mutual trust and steadfast support on all issues of core national interest,” it said. Reviewing bilateral ties, both leaders agreed that their exceptional political understanding must now be translated into a strong economic, investment and commercial partnership. PM Shehbaz emphasised that the people of Pakistan held President Aliyev and the brotherly people of Azerbaijan in the highest esteem, the statement said. The two leaders “expressed satisfaction at the growing momentum in their multifaceted cooperation and reaffirmed their shared determination to translate the exceptional political goodwill and understanding into a mutually beneficial economic, investment, and commercial partnership”, it said. The two leaders also discussed progress on ongoing bilateral initiatives, particularly the operationalisation of the Asaan Khidmat Centre in Islamabad , modelled on Azerbaijan’s ASAN Khidmet service delivery system. They described the centre as an example of the practical benefits of bilateral cooperation for the people of Pakistan, the PMO said. At PM Shehbaz’s request, President Aliyev agreed to extend Azerbaijan’s full support and expertise for expanding the Asaan Khidmat network across Pakistan. The prime minister thanked the Azerbaijani president for the gesture, describing it as another manifestation of his country’s enduring friendship and solidarity with Pakistan. The two leaders also exchanged views on the evolving regional and international situation and stressed the need for continued consultations and coordination on matters of mutual interest, the statement read. The prime minister briefed President Aliyev on Pakistan’s diplomatic outreach and efforts to promote peace, dialogue and de-escalation in the region. President Aliyev appreciated Pakistan’s constructive diplomatic efforts to facilitate dialogue and mediation, acknowledging their importance for regional peace and stability, according to the PMO. The conversation concluded with both leaders reaffirming their commitment to strengthening bilateral cooperation and transforming their strategic partnership into a lasting relationship of shared progress and prosperity, the statement added. PM Shehbaz also took to X to post about the telephone conversation. “We reaffirmed the enduring friendship and strategic partnership between Pakistan and Azerbaijan, and our resolve to translate our strong bilateral ties into greater economic, investment and trade cooperation,” he said. The two leaders last spoke by phone on May 12, when they discussed regional developments and efforts to restore peace in the Middle East, while reaffirming the strong fraternal ties between Pakistan and Azerbaijan. PM Shehbaz last visited Azerbaijan in May 2025, when the two leaders pledged to diversify their strategic partnership through investment in mutually beneficial areas. They also reviewed bilateral relations and expressed satisfaction over the growing cooperation between the two countries.

items.title: Boutiques des Allées du Centenaire : les mannequins de vitrine séduisent la clientèle
items.description: Un pantalon, une robe ou un bustier bien mis en valeur permet à une boutique de vêtements d'optimiser ses ventes. Le recours à des égéries restant inaccessible pour la plupart des commerçants du Boulevard Mamadou Dia (Allées du Centenaire) à Dakar, ces derniers se tournent vers les mannequins de vitrine. Bien plus que de simples éléments de décoration, ces supports s'avèrent être de véritables atouts commerciaux. Sur le boulevard Mamadou Dia de Dakar, les mannequins de vitrine envahissent la devanture de nombreux magasins de vêtements. Il est quasiment impossible d'y échapper du regard : bas de corps, bustes, mannequins trois-quarts ou répliques grandeur nature s'alignent sur plusieurs mètres le long des Allées du Centenaire. Debout sur leurs socles ou suspendus aux plafonds des boutiques, ils attirent l'œil tout en encombrant l'espace. En effet, pour les piétons qui cherchent à fuir les rayons mordants d'un soleil agressif de fin septembre, ces mannequins s'avèrent gênants. Pour cheminer à l'ombre des nombreux arbres qui surplombent la rue, il faut sans cesse les contourner. A lire aussi : Dakar à l’heure des JOJ : au cœur du marché Sandaga, le commerce affûte ses armes Du côté des vendeurs, le constat est tout autre. Mamadou Diouf considère ces figures de plastique comme de précieux alliés. Tout en négociant sans relâche, un exercice incontournable dans le métier, cet homme vante ses articles d'une voix chuintante. Son client, un revendeur, finit par accepter son offre : 40.000 FCfa pour une douzaine de robes. « Si les gens aiment ces robes au point de les acheter, c'est parce qu'elles sont bien exposées. Et cela, c'est grâce aux mannequins », affirme-t-il en glissant des billets de 10.000 FCfa dans son sac banane. Dans la boutique voisine, Mamy Sarr partage cet avis. Accoudée sur un gros paquet de vêtements, elle achève une conversation téléphonique qui semble porter sur une commande. Le fil coupé, elle explique avec aisance : « Les mannequins aident les clients à se projeter. Ils voient le rendu du vêtement porté avant de l'acheter, ce qui guide leur choix ». Dans son magasin, de grands miroirs fixés aux murs apportent de la profondeur. Entre les reflets des lumières blanches, les mannequins roses suspendus au plafond et les trois vendeurs de l'échoppe, une cliente fait son entrée. Elle s'arrête devant une figurine pour admirer la robe bleue qu'elle arbore. Pour cette cliente nommée Khadija, voir la pièce portée est déterminant : « D'ailleurs, cela évite aux vendeurs de voir les clients essayer tous les vêtements avant d'acheter », ajoute-t-elle après avoir réglé sa facture. Mamy Sarr approuve d'un hochement de tête entre deux négociations : « Cela permet de garder les habits propres. C'est bien plus hygiénique », précise la dame, son foulard noir et blanc rabattu sur le côté. Tout au long de ces échanges, les mannequins restent imperturbables malgré la brise fraîche qui souffle sur les Allées du Centenaire. Dans la boutique de Moustapha Diouf, ils semblent observer en silence le spectacle bruyant de la circulation. Plus que bénéfique Leur regard semble cristallisé dans le plastique : ces mannequins, le plus souvent à l'effigie d'un corps de femme, ont été achetés entre 45.000 et 50.000 FCfa l'unité pour les modèles complets. Des tarifs élevés, mais qui en valent la peine selon Moustapha. « Les mannequins aident à attirer plus de clients. Ils font aussi gagner du temps, car l'acheteur n'a plus besoin d'essayer le vêtement pour se projeter », explique le vendeur, le regard fixe. « De plus, ils sont très résistants », poursuit-il après avoir bu quelques gorgées d'eau. Quant aux mannequins en forme de buste ou s'arrêtant aux cuisses, ils s'obtiennent entre 1.000 et 1.500 FCfa, indique Malick, commerçant dans une boutique située à quelques mètres de celle de Moustapha Diouf. Derrière son comptoir en verre qui laisse entrevoir tout son stock de tissus, Malick, arborant une coupe en dégradé, est penché sur son téléphone pendant que ses deux collègues s'occupent de la clientèle. Ici, ce sont plus d'une centaine de mannequins roses qui sont plaqués contre les murs, achetés à des prix variables. « Les modèles sans tête coûtent 35.000 FCfa l'unité. Pour ceux qui en ont une, il faut compter près de 50.000 FCfa », précise Malick en désignant du doigt chaque modèle. Vêtu d'un t-shirt gris, il considère ces dépenses comme un investissement particulièrement rentable. « Nous exposons nos produits de la meilleure manière possible, ce qui séduit fortement la clientèle », confie-t-il en se caressant la barbe. Lamine SARR (Stagiaire)

items.title: Anthropic AI model sent fake murder tip to US police in Philadelphia
items.description: An artificial intelligence model developed by Anthropic submitted a fabricated tip about an unsolved homicide to Philadelphia police, authorities said on Friday, criticising the company for taking two months to report the incident. The Philadelphia Police Department said the false submission was made in July through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, a public website where people can share information about unsolved killings. According to Anthropic’s account, as relayed by police, the model was running a test that involved interacting with randomly selected websites when it reached the site and filed false information about an unsolved murder. The AI model presented itself as someone who might have knowledge of the case. The incident echoed other recent cases of unintended behaviour involving AI models, including one where an OpenAI agent undergoing a security evaluation broke out of its testing environment and breached systems at AI platform Hugging Face. Anthropic’s breaches have prompted the White House to mandate that AI companies notify and correct security incidents, news outlet Axios reported citing administration officials. “This notification and remediation process is not optional … It is a critical national security obligation,” White House Super Intelligence Force leaders said in a statement to Axios . The episode heightened concerns about the industry’s increased use of AI agents, systems programmed to take multi-step actions without human supervision. Anthropic published a report on Friday outlining multiple types of “unintended” actions that its models have taken, including the incident involving the Philadelphia Police Department website. The report said other organisations impacted included the White House and other US government agencies. The newly revealed incidents “had minimal real-world impact” and were “significantly less severe” than other cybersecurity incidents previously reported, Anthropic said. ‘Unacceptable’ delay The company outlined four categories of incidents that it found during an internal review of its Claude model: exploiting “basic” coding flaws, submitting forms on websites, bypassing requirements for tokens or fees, and using short URLs to get around other limits. Anthropic has turned off internet access for Claude during all internal testing for now “until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures … reliably catch behaviours like these,” the report said. Philadelphia police said the phoney tip, dated July 18, was flagged as spam and never reached the department’s Real-Time Crime Centre for vetting. They added that there was no sign that police systems had been breached or department data compromised. Anthropic discovered the incident on September 28, shut down the automated testing process responsible and added a new validation step for future tests, police said. The company alerted the department on October 7, and the two sides met the following day. “The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable,” the department said. Police said their safeguards had limited the impact, but that these “do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide”. “Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers,” the statement added.

items.title: La Beach demolition: Senyo Hosi condemns lack of consultation
items.description: Convener of the OneGhana Movement, Senyo Hosi, has criticised the demolition of La Beach, saying the exercise was carried out without proper consultation with the Ga people and threatens the livelihoods of thousands who depend on the area. He said the beach was not merely a recreational facility but an important part of the area’s socio-economic, tourism and entertainment infrastructure, supporting the livelihoods of thousands of people. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, October 10, Mr Hosi said the Ga people had made significant sacrifices towards Ghana’s development, including giving up their land for the establishment of the national capital. He expressed concern that the community was progressively losing influence in its own traditional space despite its historical contribution to the country. “My Ga people have been very kind to this country. We’ve given up our land, we’ve given this country its capital, even to the detriment of our own identity,” he said. Mr Hosi said the least the Ga people deserved was respect, appreciation and recognition for their contribution to national development. He described as depressing the situation in which chiefs had held a press conference to announce developments affecting the community without what he considered adequate consultation. “To see my chiefs sit there in a press conference and claim a thing like this has happened without any form of consultation is depressing and is disrespectful,” he said. Livelihoods at stake Mr Hosi said La Beach had served as an important source of livelihood for people who depended on its commercial and recreational activities for their economic survival. According to him, the beach had grown into a significant part of the local economy, with vendors and other operators relying on the activities there to earn a living. He said the state had also benefited financially from activities at the beach, including the collection of revenue to support local councils. Mr Hosi argued that any decision to reorganise the area must take into account the economic consequences for the people who depended on it. “This has become a critical part of our socio-economic infrastructure, our tourism infrastructure, our entertainment and recreational infrastructure,” he said. He added that he was concerned about the thousands of Ga people whose livelihoods and economic activities depended on the beach. Questions consistency of enforcement Mr Hosi also questioned the consistency of enforcement against structures along the coast, asking why action was being taken in some areas while other developments appeared to remain untouched. He specifically raised questions about Sandbox Beach, asking whether it had obtained a lease and whether the same standards were being applied to other operators along the coast. “Did you go and bring Sandbox? Is it because of the political weight that’s behind it? Have they taken a lease from you people? How about the other people?” he asked. He called on the relevant authorities to demonstrate fairness and transparency in the enforcement of rules governing coastal developments. Mr Hosi further questioned why the authorities had allowed the area to develop over the years if the structures were considered illegal. He maintained that if the state intended to streamline activities along the coast, it should develop a clear plan and apply it consistently across affected areas, including other parts of the Central Region. Calls for due process Mr Hosi said the state had a responsibility to regulate the beach and determine how the area should be developed, but insisted that such decisions must follow legitimate and constitutional processes. He argued that La Beach had existed for years as a recognised destination for recreation and entertainment, rather than an informal settlement that had emerged without the knowledge of the authorities. He questioned why the state had not used its regulatory powers and the revenue it collected to establish a clear framework for managing the area. According to him, a proper planning process would have helped prevent the current situation and ensured that the interests of affected communities were considered. “If you have a legitimate reason, go through a legitimate and constitutional process. Don’t be arbitrary. Don’t be unfair. Don’t be disrespectful to my people,” he said. Mr Hosi expressed concern about the demolition of La Beach, saying the Ga people’s historical contributions to Ghana must be respected and considered in decisions affecting their land and livelihoods. He called for an approach that balances the state’s responsibility to regulate coastal areas with fairness, transparency and respect for the people whose lives and economic activities are tied to La Beach.

items.title: Campagne agricole : Plus de 1 000 tonnes de récoltes attendues dans les établissements pénitentiaires du Burkina Faso
items.description: En visite sur le site du Centre Pénitentiaire Agricole de Baporo ce 9 octobre 2026, le ministre de la Justice, Me Edasso Rodrigue Bayala, a salué l’engagement des pensionnaires et du personnel pénitentiaire, tout en soulignant le rôle de l’accompagnement gouvernemental dans les performances enregistrées. Ce centre pénitentiaire agricole de Baporo attend une production de 550,2 tonnes de céréales et de légumineuses pour la campagne agricole 2026-2027. À Baporo, la campagne agricole concerne notamment le riz, le maïs, le sorgho, le niébé et le sésame. Le riz occupe 90 hectares, pour une production attendue de 225 tonnes. Le maïs est cultivé sur 85 hectares, avec 212 tonnes attendues, tandis que le sorgho s’étend sur 63 hectares pour une prévision de 94 tonnes. Le niébé occupe 20 hectares, pour 16 tonnes attendues, et le sésame 5 hectares, pour une production estimée à 3,2 tonnes. Au total, les prévisions font état de 550,2 tonnes de production sur le site. Le ministre a pu constater l’avancement des récoltes de riz et participer au battage aux côtés des pensionnaires. Une dynamique portée par plusieurs ministères-©Faso7 Pour Me Edasso Rodrigue Bayala, les résultats de Baporo ne peuvent être dissociés de la coopération entre les départements ministériels concernés. Le ministère de la Justice bénéficie notamment de l’appui technique du ministère chargé de l’Agriculture, qui intervient dans l’accompagnement des producteurs et la mise à disposition de compétences et d’intrants agricoles. « C’est l’ensemble des efforts du gouvernement qui donne le résultat que vous avez présenté » , a déclaré le ministre de la Justice, qui a particulièrement salué l’appui du ministre d’État, chargé de l'Agriculture, qui s’est lui-même rendu à Baporo pour lancer la campagne. Selon lui, cette collaboration doit permettre d’accroître les capacités de production des établissements pénitentiaires et de contribuer progressivement à l’autosuffisance alimentaire. Il a indiqué que, depuis 2024, le ministère de la Justice n’acquiert plus de céréales pour assurer la prise en charge alimentaire des pensionnaires dans les établissements concernés. Les dépenses se concentrent désormais sur les condiments et d’autres besoins complémentaires. Le ministre a également mis en avant l’évolution des superficies exploitées à Baporo. D’environ 15 hectares exploitables en 2022-2023, le centre est passé à plus de 300 hectares avec plus de 260 hectares emblavés pour la campagne actuelle. « Nous sommes très satisfaits aujourd’hui parce que nous sommes déjà aux récoltes pour le riz, et même le maïs est déjà à maturité » , a-t-il déclaré, tout en reconnaissant que les poches de sécheresse enregistrées ont affecté les cultures. Plus de 1 000 tonnes attendues dans les établissements pénitentiaires-©Faso7 À l’échelle nationale, l’administration pénitentiaire prévoit une production de 1 014,7 tonnes pour la campagne agricole 2026-2027, sur une superficie totale de 574 hectares répartis entre plusieurs établissements. Amidou Zerbo, Directeur de la production pénitentiaire et de la formation professionnelle, a expliqué que les prévisions reposent sur une évaluation des superficies exploitables et des capacités de production des différentes maisons d’arrêt. Dix principaux centres ont été retenus pour intensifier les activités agricoles, avec une dotation en intrants, notamment des semences, de l’engrais NPK et de l’urée et en labour gratuit, en partenariat avec le ministère en charge de l’Agriculture. Outre Baporo, qui représente à lui seul 550,2 tonnes attendues, Banfora prévoit 150 tonnes sur 76 hectares. Les établissements de Sourgoubila, de Bobo-Dioulasso et Gaoua affichent chacun une prévision de 50 tonnes, respectivement sur 42, 40 et 20 hectares. Les autres sites contribuent également à l’objectif national. Pour Me Edasso Rodrigue Bayala, les prévisions actuelles témoignent d’une progression importante de la production pénitentiaire. Il a toutefois insisté sur la nécessité de préserver les récoltes jusqu’à leur stockage afin que les efforts consentis pendant les semis et l’entretien des cultures se traduisent effectivement en résultats. La production comme levier de réinsertion-©Faso7 Au-delà des rendements agricoles, la visite a également porté sur les conditions de vie et les perspectives de réinsertion des pensionnaires. Le ministre a rappelé que la nouvelle orientation pénitentiaire vise à permettre aux détenus de participer à des activités productives et d’acquérir des compétences utiles à leur retour dans la société. « La prison aussi doit permettre de produire, non seulement pour prendre en charge les pensionnaires, mais pour contribuer à l’autosuffisance alimentaire dans notre pays » , a-t-il souligné. Il a annoncé que des ateliers de formation en élevage, en pisciculture, en soudure et en menuiserie devraient compléter les activités agricoles. Selon lui, ces apprentissages doivent permettre aux pensionnaires de sortir du centre avec des compétences supplémentaires et de meilleures perspectives d’insertion. Le texte sur les travaux d'intérêt général connaîtra des innovations-©Faso7 Le ministre a par ailleurs évoqué la situation des pensionnaires qui ne bénéficient pas encore du dispositif de travail d’intérêt général (TIG). Il leur a annoncé que le cadre juridique en cours de révision devra permettre d’élargir l’accès à ce dispositif. « Le bénéfice du TIG ne sera plus limité aux seules personnes condamnées avant l’entrée en vigueur de la loi » , a-t-il expliqué. Prenant la parole au nom des pensionnaires, leur représentant a remercié les autorités pour les initiatives engagées et salué les possibilités offertes par le travail agricole. Il a assuré que les pensionnaires et leurs encadreurs restent mobilisés pour atteindre les objectifs de production fixés. La visite a également conduit Me Edasso Rodrigue Bayala dans la nouvelle unité de détention de 500 places, équipée de lits, de matelas, de ventilateurs, de douches et d’une laverie. Le ministre y a donné des instructions en vue d’améliorer davantage les conditions de séjour des pensionnaires. Les résultats agricoles attendus illustrent ainsi une approche qui associe production, formation et réinsertion. La poursuite de la collaboration entre les ministères, l’administration pénitentiaire et les pensionnaires sera déterminante pour consolider ces acquis et faire des établissements pénitentiaires des acteurs de la production nationale. Josué TIENDREBEOGO Faso7 L’article Campagne agricole : Plus de 1 000 tonnes de récoltes attendues dans les établissements pénitentiaires du Burkina Faso est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

En effet, grâce au contrôle systématique effectué à travers le fichier IRAPOL (Identification, Rapprochement et Analyse de Police), les engins admis en fourrière font l’objet de vérifications permettant notamment d’identifier ceux qui sont déclarés volés et répertoriés dans la base de données. Heureux de retrouver leurs engins, les bénéficiaires ont exprimé leur satisfaction et adressé leurs remerciements à la Police Municipale pour le travail accompli. Le Camarade Président de la Délégation Spéciale de la Commune de Ouagadougou a félicité la Police Municipale pour les résultats obtenus notamment la découverte des engins déclarés volés et leur restitution à leurs propriétaires légitimes. Il a salué les efforts déployés par les agents ainsi que l’utilisation du système IRAPOL, qui contribue au renforcement de l’efficacité des actions de la Police Municipale au service de la population. La Police Municipale, toujours plus proche de vous ! items.title: Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 15 people
items.description: Russia has attacked the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia with five glide bombs, killing at least 15 people including three children, President Volodymyr Zelensky and emergency services have said. The glide bombs hit residential buildings in the south-eastern city. At least 16 other people were injured in the attack, with more still missing and believed to be under the rubble after the strike on Saturday morning. Zelensky said 13 other regions had also been hit overnight, adding: “Our responses to [these] Russian strikes will come”. The Russian attacks happened just hours after President Donald Trump announced a deal to import Russian diesel into the US. Photos and videos from the site of one of the strikes show an apartment block mostly destroyed. “The ground floor was hit, and the floors above just collapsed,” acting Mayor Regina Kharchenko told Ukrainian television, speaking from the scene. She said more than 80 workers were involved in ongoing search and rescue operations which are expected to continue throughout the day. The rescuers regularly stop to listen for any noises made by survivors who could be under the rubble. Kharchenko said Russia had struck at “our very heart” and “our littlest ones” were among those killed, adding that their deaths were “awful grief for their families. For the city.” Zelensky has heavily criticised Trump’s diesel deal with Russia, calling it a gift to President Vladimir Putin that amounts to “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”. More recently, in his response to the overnight strikes, he said “Russia interprets any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly continue the war. “Russia must understand that the war needs to be stopped, and for that, it must feel its losses,” he wrote on X. Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months, as the war between the two countries drags on. Zaporizhzhia is a major regional centre with more than 700,000 residents. It is located less than 10 miles (16 km) from the front line and is frequently attacked by Russian drones and missiles. The latest strikes on the city comes amid a sharp increase in the number of Russian attacks that are causing higher numbers of civilian casualties. On Thursday, at least 33 people were killed in another Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in Kramatorsk, in the eastern Donetsk region. The day before, 22 people including five children died as a Russian missile hit an apartment block in the town of Pryluky, east of Kyiv. According to the UN, the number of civilian casualties in Ukraine jumped by 55% in the first eight months of this year. Russia has also targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since Putin launched a full-scale invasion in 2022. For its part, Ukraine has attacked Russia’s infrastructure – with the latest being strikes on data centres owned by tech giant Yandex.
